Title: 2 quick questions. Forfeit and theft of vitae.

Messages.Author: Jason
Messages.Body:
First: I used to think blood stolen from theft of vitae couldn't
immediatly be used to heal damage from the same strike phase...
apparantly that the Final Nights rulebook states specifically that you
can.

So the question is: is the following legal?

Close range.
Vamp A with zero blood declares strike "Steal 2 blood"
Vamp B with 2 blood declares strike "hands"

After this round Vamp A has 1 blood left and is still ready, and Vamp
B is empty but still ready.

Correct?

Question 2:

This weekend we played a few games and I had a pretty nasty assamites
deck going strong. In fact, in our 3 player game, I toporised and
diablerised every single vampire on the table. (it was a QUI FOR
Tariq, Tergerius deck)

As I was slowly going through my Prey's 8 pool, each of my four
minions bleeding for 1, my predator (or grand-prey) was fed up with me
as I didn't give him a chance to do anything, So in spite he decided
to resign and cede his victory point to my prey... just so I couldn't
say that I swept the table. We mentioned that the rules made no
provisions for this as he still had 90% of his library, so he
influenced himself out.

As this was friendly play, that was fine, but in a tournament how
would this be handled?

Jason

Messages.Author: Halcyan 2
Messages.Body:
>You don't know that. The judge doesn't know that. Since collusion is
>"secret", the only way to detect it is if you appear to be giving the game
>away
>to someone. I know that I remember LSJ saying something in the past few
>months
>about your obligation to try to win. If you do not try to win and you hand
>the
>game over to someone else, it little matters whether or not you agreed
>beforehand to do so, it's still cheating.

You are required to win in general, but it can get a bit hazy. The simple model
is: 1.) Try to maximize table wins, 2.) Try to maximize VP's, and a distant 3.)
Try to maximize tournament points.

If you can, you should try to maximize table wins but if you can't get a table
win, you should still try to maximize VP's. Now it *is* possible however to be
in a no-win situation. If you are in a no-win situation, LSJ has explicitly
said that you can be ousted in the manner of your choosing. A good example is
if you have 3 pool left, you're bled for 6 by your predator and you have an
Archon Investigation. You're ousted either way. Is playing the AI doing
something out of spite? Is the better to "let" him win w/o losing a minion?
Should you roll over or be a really nasty speed bump? (There is no right
answer).

Of course it can get hazy in some situations. Is it better to have 1 VP and be
third in a 2-2-1 split? Or to be tied for second with 0 VP in a 5-0-0 split? Is
"winning" dependent on TW's, VP's, TP's, or ordinal ranking?

Another example that I asked to LSJ a while back (and he confirmed) is that:
say your deck is really kick-@$$ and has already ousted three Methusalehs (in a
5-player game). You already have 3 VP's and the TW. There's nothing preventing
you from letting the remaining Methusaleh withdraw out of pity, or even ousting
yourself to give that individual 2 VP. Either way, you have the Table Win and
have won. You have to play to win and you have done that.

The distant third I mentioned is that technically, you should also try to
maximize Tournament Points (assuming the tournament is actually using them.
I've seen quite a few that don't). In this case, there really is a (very)
slight advantage to being ousted last. I guess this is the technical
justification for "being a difficult speedbump" and in most circumstances, I
would rather be ousted last than first (if someone's sweeping). But honestly,
very few people ever bother worrying about TP's. Focusing too much of it would
make the game rather pathetic since you would technically have to *beg* people
to keep you alive for "just one more turn" on the hope that someone else who is
low on pool is ousted first. At times, I'd rather be ousted with dignity and
done with it than to waste my time begging for pool and intercept to delay the
inevitable. (Nothing wrong with asking for help but in this case the end is
inevitable).

As I said earlier, if you're in a no-win situation, you can choose how you go
out. Which also means that (out of spite or strategy) you can even Dramatic
Upheaval yourself to give your VP to someone more deserving. For example, one
time in a friendly game, I was getting pounded on by a weenie potence deck. By
grandpredator was gracious enough to help me several times (rescuing several
vampires from torpor, etc.). But in the end, I knew I was going to get ousted
no matter what (one pool, predator had plenty of pool and lots of minions
compared to my one). I was in a no-win situation so I figured I might as well
Dramatic Upheaval to give my grandpredator (who had helped me so much) a VP.
Besides, I had promised him that I'd do something nice in return! =)

Of course, in any of these situations, you must always be vigilant for
collusion since it is indeed possible. But nothing in the rules prohibits you
from doing any of these (as long as it's not pre-determined collusion).

So the point is, in general, you have to play to win (which does not always
mean maximizing VP's). If you are in a no-win situation, you can choose how you
want to be ousted.

Halcyan 2

So, now every stupid play you make is cheating. Any action you take
can hand the game to someone else. It is simply a matter of being
able to isolate that one action. Was it bringing out the Hunting
Ground that gave your prey the game, or was it cheating?

Wow, do you really work this hard to not know the meanings
of the words?

Cheating (per www.m-w.com):

"to violate rules dishonestly"

There are no rules against transferring out. There are no rules
against stupid play. Where there is no rules violation, there is
no cheating.

> If I agree beforehand to transfer out, then it's collusion,
> but if I don't agree beforehand, it's not illegal???

It's not illegal to transfer out. There is no rule against it,
that another word you might want to look up when you get a chance.

Illegal (per www.m-w.com):

"not sanctioned by official rules"

Specifically allowed, in fact encouraged by the official rules,
section 7 of the online rulebook reads:

"During your influence phase, you may spend your transfers
as follows:
Spend one transfer to move one blood counter from your pool
to a vampire in your uncontrolled region."

There is never a time where this rule is over-ridden, either
in the regular rules or in the tournament rules. Transferring
out is sanctioned by the official rules.

> How does the judge know what I agreed to beforehand.

She doesn't know what you agreed to beforehand. There is
no viable way to enforce a rule on collusion, because you
cannot punish stupid play, nor can you prohibit the actions
allowed to you by the game UNTIL you make a rule to do so.
There is no such rule about transferring out.

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:


It is not obviously a violation of that rule, as has been explained.

If you will lose (not gain any more VPs) whether you transfer yourself
out or not, then you are free to "not win and not gain any more VPs" by
transferring yourself out, just as you are free to "not win and not gain
any more VPs" by not tranferring yourself out. There is no criterion
that makes one losing course of action preferable over another losing
course of action. If there is a non-losing course of action, however,
that is a different story. In the case in question, however, the
player attempting to transfer is identified as not able to win any
VPs anyway.

Fine.

Naturally, if you change the assumptions for a given situation, the
"answers" to the problem may change as well.

I've often said that it is very difficult to be in a truly lost
position (i.e., one in which it would be legal to transfer
yourself out).

That, however, doesn't change the fact that when a player is
in a truly lost position, she is free to transfer out (just as
she is free to lose in whatever other fashion is avilable).

> Anarch Revolts, cross-table votes, anything like that could do it. But if you
> oust yourself, you have 0 chance of that happening. Are you saying that a 1%
> chance doesn't count, or does a 1% chance always require that you stay in the
> game?

I wasn't saying either. Neither statement is all that interesting, however,
since it is impossible to evaluate your chances like that. The rules allow
for judges to judge such things. So they do. If the judge feels that the
player cannot (reasonably) do any better than her intended course of action,
then she is free to pursue her intended course of action.

So if the judge feels that the player is in a truly lost position, then
the player is allowed to transfer out. If the judge feels that the player
could reasonably gain a VP (or a win) by not transferring out, then the
player is not allowed to transfer out.

It was the deck with which I won storyline Chicago. You should be able to find
it by searching Google, or if yoritomo jiriki still has his storyline page up.
But it was a pretty standard Lasombra S&B. Even dedicated intercept decks have
a hard time packing enough to stop a true S&B. Because all I need is a bleed
modifier and a bunch of stealth. He needs a bunch of intercept *and* a bunch
of combat. Since most decks don't have a bunch of stealth, it's generally
advantageous to minimize the intercept needed, just so you don't jam. In an
environment that is not *predominantly* stealthy, an intercept deck which can
survive usually is not able to survive against particularly stealthy decks. I
think this is because intercept is not, on average, more effective than
stealth. Enhanced Senses is about on a par with Lost in Crowd, and so on down
the line for OBF versus AUS. You don't gain an advantage for being reactive
versus proactive, and thus do not offset the inherent disadvantage that being
reactive brings. (That is, if I can state it more clearly, being reactive is
generally "worse" than being proactive, but reactive cards are not generally
stronger than proactive cards, thus the proactive deck will generally win on a
level playing field.)

to

Of course they care to do this. Every victory point they don't get is one VP
closer to losing the table. And around here even non-vote decks occasionally
pass votes that they think can be passed with politics (mostly only *my* decks,
but still...). But with the average of 2 vote decks per table, chances are
that someone *can* keep you in the game if they draw correctly and have the
support of the table.

But there are just so few conditions where a person has *no* chance, why even
worry about it? Besides, influencing yourself out in spite is not really a
reasonable criteria for deciding the fate of a tournament, now is it?

> > But it's clear that conceding does not accomplish the tournament goals,
> namely
> > a) maximizing table wins and b) maximizing victory points.
>
> Your statement is only correct if the player doing the conceding believs that
> they have a REASONABLE chance of being able to obtain a VP. If they don't,
> your statemtn doesn't apply, and that player is free to choose the manner of
> their ousting.
>

No, no, no. That's not true. If there is even an infinitesimal chance of
getting a VP, then self-ousting will minimize your VP's. It will ensure that
you cannot gain another VP no matter what happens. As long as the chance is
not 0, you must try to maximize your victory points. You're going to say that
it's silly to require the chance of winning to be exactly 0, for reasons
similar to, "the chance of the world still existing from moment to moment is
not even 0." And I'll agree. Which is why it's simpler to just say that you
can't self-oust. By self-ousting, you are giving up on trying to win, you are
minimizing your VP's and you are breaking the rules of a tournament, plain and
simple. On top of that, you are being unsportsmanlike and are unfairly
upsetting the balance of the table. Granted, you can't legislate being a good
sport, but it's just convenient that being a poor loser in this situation is
also against the rules.
